course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
sessionGoal: Students should be able to find eigenvalues/eigenvectors and explain that an eigenvector keeps its direction under a matrix.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start with the meaning: Av=λv means A only stretches or flips v.
Do Problem 1 to show triangular matrices are fast.
Do Problem 2 for the full characteristic polynomial method.
Do Problem 3 to show how to test whether a given vector is an eigenvector.
sayThisFirst: An eigenvector is a direction that does not rotate under A.
The eigenvalue is the stretch factor in that direction.
To find eigenvectors, plug each λ into A-λI and solve the homogeneous system.
boardPlan: Write Av=λv and explain it in one sentence.
End with the shortcut: to test a given v, compute Av and see if it is a multiple of v.
keyFormulas: Triangular matrix eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.
commonMistakes: Allowing v=0 as an eigenvector. The zero vector is never an eigenvector.
Finding eigenvalues but forgetting to find eigenspaces.
Plugging λ into A instead of A-λI.
Thinking repeated eigenvalues automatically give enough eigenvectors.
notationWarnings: Use λ for eigenvalues and v for eigenvectors.
Write \(\operatorname{Nul}(A-\lambda I)\), not just \(A-\lambda I\), when describing the eigenspace.

problems.title: Eigenvalues and eigenspaces of a triangular matrix
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \[A=\begin{bmatrix}3&1&0\\0&3&0\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}.\] Find the eigenvalues and a basis for each eigenspace.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: because this matrix is triangular, eigenvalues are on the diagonal. We still need to solve for eigenspaces.

drawInstructions: Write that λ=3 has algebraic multiplicity 2.
Draw two direction arrows: one for the λ=3 eigenspace and one for λ=2.

walkthrough.label: Read eigenvalues from the diagonal
walkthrough.latex: Since \(A\) is triangular, the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: \(3,3,2\). So \(\lambda=3\) and \(\lambda=2\).

walkthrough.label: Find the eigenspace for λ=3
walkthrough.latex: \[A-3I=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&-1\end{bmatrix}.\] This gives \(y=0\) and \(z=0\), with \(x\) free. So \[E_3=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0)\}.\]

walkthrough.label: Find the eigenspace for λ=2
walkthrough.latex: \[A-2I=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}.\] This gives \(y=0\) and \(x=0\), with \(z\) free. So \[E_2=\operatorname{span}\{(0,0,1)\}.\]

commonMistakes: Stopping after reading the diagonal and not finding eigenspaces.
Assuming λ=3 must have a two-dimensional eigenspace because it appears twice.
Forgetting that eigenvectors cannot be zero.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 5 for eigenvalues and eigenspaces.

problems.title: Full 2 by 2 eigenvalue/eigenvector calculation
problems.studentPromptLatex: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \[A=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}.\]
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: this is the standard method. Characteristic polynomial first, eigenspaces second.

drawInstructions: Draw two lines through the origin: one in direction (2,1), one in direction (1,-1).
Label the first direction λ=5 and the second λ=2.
Say these directions are preserved by A.

walkthrough.label: Find eigenvectors for λ=5
walkthrough.latex: \[A-5I=\begin{bmatrix}-1&2\\1&-2\end{bmatrix}.\] The equation is \(-x+2y=0\), so \(x=2y\). A basis vector is \((2,1)\).

walkthrough.label: Find eigenvectors for λ=2
walkthrough.latex: \[A-2I=\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\1&1\end{bmatrix}.\] The equation is \(x+y=0\), so \(x=-y\). A basis vector is \((1,-1)\).

commonMistakes: Making a sign error in A-λI.
Factoring the characteristic polynomial correctly but forgetting eigenvectors.
Using the same eigenvector for both eigenvalues.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 5 for full eigenvalue/eigenvector practice.

problems.title: Choose a parameter so a given vector is an eigenvector
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \[A=\begin{bmatrix}2&k\\3&5\end{bmatrix},\qquad v=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.\] Find \(k\) so that \(v\) is an eigenvector of \(A\). Then find the corresponding eigenvalue.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: if v is an eigenvector, then Av must point in exactly the same direction as v.

drawInstructions: Draw v along the line y=x.
Say Av must land on the same line y=x.
Use the two entries of Av to force them to be equal.

walkthrough.label: Force Av to be a multiple of v
walkthrough.latex: Since \(v=(1,1)\), any multiple of \(v\) has equal entries. So we need \(2+k=8\).

commonMistakes: Only checking one coordinate of Av.
Forgetting that Av must be a scalar multiple of v, not just any vector.
Saying k is the eigenvalue. k is a matrix entry; λ is the eigenvalue.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 5 for eigenvector tests.

wrapUpQuestions: What does Av=λv mean in words?
Why is the zero vector not an eigenvector?

linksToWebsite.note: Practice Lab Section(s) 5 for more practice.

qualityControlNotes: Checked triangular eigenspaces for λ=3 and λ=2.
Checked parameter problem: k=6 gives Av=(8,8).
reviewSummary: Session 11 focuses on eigenvalues as stretch factors and eigenspaces as preserved directions.

open.title: Start with a question
say: Every time you multiply a vector by a matrix, two things can happen: it changes length, and it turns.
Most vectors do both. Today is about the special directions that never turn. Those are eigenvectors, and they are the directions where a matrix is at its simplest.

ask.q: If I hit a vector with a matrix, what two things can happen to it?
ask.a: It can get longer or shorter, and it can change direction.

write: eigenvector: a direction A does not turn

idea.title: An eigenvector only gets stretched
say: Take \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). It doubles the x-coordinate and leaves y alone.
Arrows on the x-axis just get twice as long. Arrows on the y-axis do not change at all. Every other arrow tilts toward the x-axis.
So the two axes are the eigenvector directions, with stretch factors 2 and 1. That is all an eigenvalue is: the stretch factor along a direction that does not turn.
draw: Draw axes and a light unit circle.
Draw an arrow on the x-axis and its image twice as long on the same line. Label it λ = 2.
Draw an arrow on the y-axis; its image is the same arrow. Label it λ = 1.
Draw a diagonal arrow and its image tilted toward the x-axis. Write next to it: turned, so not an eigenvector.

ask.q: Why do we insist that v is not the zero vector?
ask.a: A0 = λ0 for every number λ, so the zero vector would make every λ an eigenvalue. It carries no information.

ask.q: Someone hands you a matrix and a vector. How do you check if the vector is an eigenvector?
ask.a: Compute Av and see whether it is a scalar multiple of v.

bridge.say: To find them, rewrite the equation. We want a nonzero solution v, which only happens when A − λI is singular.

launch.say: The first one is quick if you notice the shape of the matrix. Find the eigenvalues, then a basis for each eigenspace.
circulate: Who reads the eigenvalues straight off the diagonal? Ask them why that works.
Who stops after the eigenvalues? Point back at the question: it also asks for eigenspaces.

askFirst.q: What is special about this matrix?
askFirst.a: It is upper triangular, so det(A − λI) is just the product of the diagonal entries: (3 − λ)(3 − λ)(2 − λ).

steps.say: A − λI is still triangular, so its determinant is the product down the diagonal. The eigenvalues are right there: 3, 3 and 2.

ask.q: 3 shows up twice. What does that tell us, and what does it not tell us?
ask.a: λ = 3 has algebraic multiplicity 2. It does not yet tell us how many independent eigenvectors λ = 3 has.

steps.why: Reading the diagonal only works for triangular and diagonal matrices. Everything else needs the characteristic polynomial.

steps.say: Plug λ = 3 into A − λI, not into A. Row 1 says y = 0. Row 3 says −z = 0, so z = 0. Only x is free.

ask.q: How many free variables, so what is the dimension of E₃?
ask.a: One free variable (x), so E₃ is a line through the origin: dimension 1.

steps.why: λ = 3 appeared twice but only gave one direction. That mismatch is exactly what next session is about.

steps.say: Same move for λ = 2. The rows give x + y = 0 and y = 0, so x = y = 0 and z is free.
steps.why: Every eigenspace is a null space: \(E_\lambda=\operatorname{Nul}(A-\lambda I)\). Solving for it is the same row reduction you already know.

si11-p1.meaning: A stretches the whole x-axis by 3 and the whole z-axis by 2. The y-axis is not an eigen-direction, because the 1 above the diagonal shears it toward x. Even though 3 appears twice, it only earns one direction.

ifStuck.if: a student plugs λ into A instead of A − λI
ifStuck.then: ask what equation we are solving: (A − λI)v = 0. Subtract λ from the diagonal together.

ifStuck.if: a student says E₃ must be two-dimensional because 3 appears twice
ifStuck.then: solve it together. The number of free variables decides the dimension, not the repetition.

si11-p1.transition: Triangular matrices hand us the eigenvalues. Most matrices do not, so next we run the full recipe.

launch.say: This is the standard two-stage recipe: characteristic polynomial first, eigenvectors second. Four minutes, then we do it together.
circulate: Watch the −2 in (4 − λ)(3 − λ) − 2. It comes from the off-diagonal product 2 · 1.
When someone reaches A − 5I, check that the two rows are multiples of each other. If not, there is an arithmetic slip.

askFirst.q: Before computing anything: at most how many eigenvalues can a 2 × 2 matrix have?
askFirst.a: Two, because the characteristic polynomial has degree 2.

steps.say: Subtract λ from every diagonal entry, and only the diagonal.

ask.a: λI is λ times the identity, and the identity only has entries on the diagonal.

steps.say: Determinant of a 2 × 2 is ad − bc. Here that is (4 − λ)(3 − λ) − 2 · 1. Expand it slowly.

ask.q: What should the constant term be, as a check?
ask.a: det A = 4 · 3 − 2 · 1 = 10. The constant term of the characteristic polynomial of a 2 × 2 is det A.

steps.why: Two free checks for any 2 × 2: the λ coefficient is minus the trace (−7) and the constant is the determinant (10).

steps.say: Factor. Two numbers that multiply to 10 and add to 7: 5 and 2.

ask.q: How can you check these with no extra work?

steps.why: Sum of the eigenvalues is the trace; product is the determinant. That is the fastest check you have on an exam.

steps.say: Now λ = 5. The rows (−1, 2) and (1, −2) are multiples of each other, as they should be: A − 5I is singular. One equation is left: x = 2y.

ask.q: If the two rows gave two independent equations, what would that tell you?
ask.a: That A − 5I is invertible, so 5 is not an eigenvalue. Go back and find the arithmetic slip.

steps.why: The rows collapsing is a built-in error check.

steps.say: λ = 2: rows (2, 2) and (1, 1). So x = −y, and a basis vector is (1, −1).

si11-p2.meaning: Two lines through the origin survive A without turning. Along (2, 1) everything is stretched 5 times; along (1, −1) everything doubles. Every other vector is a mix of those two, which is why eigenvectors make A easy to understand.

ifStuck.then: they dropped the −bc term. Ask them to recompute ad − bc with b = 2 and c = 1.

ifStuck.if: a student gives the same eigenvector for both eigenvalues
ifStuck.then: plug it in. A times one vector cannot equal both 5v and 2v.

si11-p2.transition: We just found eigenvectors from scratch. Sometimes a problem hands you the vector and asks about the matrix instead.

launch.say: Different flavor: the vector is given and the matrix has an unknown. Use the definition, not the determinant.
circulate: Who computes Av first? That is the fast path.
If someone starts det(A − λI) with k inside, ask if there is a quicker test for one specific vector.

askFirst.q: If v is an eigenvector, what has to be true about Av?
askFirst.a: Av is a scalar multiple of v: it lands on the same line through the origin.

steps.say: Multiply it out. Row 1 gives 2 + k. Row 2 gives 3 + 5 = 8.

ask.q: v = (1, 1) points along the line y = x. Where does Av need to land?
ask.a: On the same line y = x, so its two entries must be equal.

steps.say: Multiples of (1, 1) always have equal entries. So both entries of Av have to match.

ask.q: Why can we not just set 2 + k equal to λ and stop?
ask.a: The second entry also has to equal λ, and it is 8. Both entries must be the same λ, and that is what pins down k.

steps.say: 2 + k = 8, so k = 6. Then Av = (8, 8) = 8v, so the eigenvalue is 8.

ask.a: No. k is an entry of the matrix; the eigenvalue is λ = 8.

si11-p3.meaning: Choosing k tilts the matrix until the line y = x becomes a direction A does not turn. With k = 6, A stretches that line by a factor of 8.

ifStuck.if: a student only checks the first coordinate
ifStuck.then: ask them to write Av = λv one entry at a time: 2 + k = λ and 8 = λ. Both have to hold.

wrap.write: Eigenvector: a nonzero direction A does not turn. Eigenvalue: its stretch factor. Find λ from det(A − λI) = 0, then v from Nul(A − λI).

exit.q: What does Av = λv mean in words?
exit.a: A only stretches (or flips) v; it does not turn it.

exit.q: Why do we solve det(A − λI) = 0?
exit.a: We need a nonzero v with (A − λI)v = 0, and that only happens when A − λI is singular.

exit.q: Why is the zero vector never an eigenvector?
exit.a: A0 = λ0 for every λ, so it tells us nothing. Eigenvectors are nonzero by definition.

wrap.next: Next session: what happens when an eigenvalue repeats but you do not get enough eigenvectors. Problem 1 was a preview.
